common_name: Royal Candles Veronica (Compact Long-Blooming Blue Speedwell)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Royal Candles produces dense, upright spikes of true blue flowers over a long summer season and reblooms readily if sheared after the first flush.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Royal Candles is a compact, sterile veronica selection producing exceptionally dense, upright spikes of vivid true-blue flowers over a long bloom season from late spring into summer, one of the truest blue colors available among perennial spike flowers. Being sterile, it never sets seed and instead channels its energy into continuous new flower spikes, and shearing spent spikes after the first flush encourages a strong rebloom later in the season. It forms a tidy, mounding clump that rarely needs division, tolerates average garden soil well, and draws bees readily, making it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for the front to middle of a sunny border.

common_name: Sunny Border Blue Veronica (Perennial Plant of the Year Deep Blue Speedwell)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Sunny Border Blue was named Perennial Plant of the Year for its long bloom season, glossy dark green foliage, and dependable performance across a wide range of conditions.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Sunny Border Blue was named the Perennial Plant Association's Perennial Plant of the Year in 1993 and remains one of the most reliable, widely grown veronica cultivars, producing dense spikes of rich violet-blue flowers over glossy, deep green, crinkled foliage from early summer well into fall with deadheading. Its exceptional garden performance and long bloom season across a wide range of soil and climate conditions have made it a benchmark perennial for sunny borders, and it draws bees and butterflies reliably throughout its bloom period. Divide the clump every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor as the center becomes congested.

common_name: Whirling Butterflies Gaura (Airy Long-Blooming White Wandflower)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Whirling Butterflies produces airy sprays of small white flowers on thin, wiry stems that dance in the slightest breeze, giving the plant its common name.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, since gaura resents wet, poorly drained soil, especially in winter. Whirling Butterflies produces masses of small, white, four-petaled flowers tinged with pink on tall, airy, wiry stems that seem to hover and flutter above the foliage like a cloud of small butterflies, blooming continuously from late spring through frost with minimal deadheading needed. Its deep taproot makes it exceptionally drought-tolerant once established but also means it resents being moved or divided, so choose its planting site carefully. It combines beautifully with bolder-textured perennials and ornamental grasses, adding lightness and movement to a sunny border.

common_name: Husker Red Penstemon (Bronze-Red Foliage Native Beardtongue)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade; Husker Red was named Perennial Plant of the Year for its striking burgundy-red foliage, a dramatic contrast to its white summer flower spikes.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade. Husker Red was named the Perennial Plant Association's Perennial Plant of the Year in 1996 for combining the tough, easygoing nature of native foxglove beardtongue with strikingly dark burgundy-red foliage that provides season-long color, topped in early summer by tall spikes of white, tubular, foxglove-like flowers tinged with pink that draw hummingbirds and bees. It is drought-tolerant once established, tolerates a wide range of soil conditions, and self-seeds modestly, though seedlings often revert toward green foliage rather than staying true burgundy-red. Deadhead spent flower spikes to maintain a tidy appearance and prevent excessive self-seeding.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Paprika requires excellent drainage and will not tolerate heavy, wet clay, particularly through summer humidity.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; heavy clay or consistently wet soil quickly kills yarrow, especially in humid summers. Paprika produces flat-topped flower clusters that open a vivid brick-red and gradually fade through shades of salmon-orange and soft gold as they age, often showing several colors on the same plant at once, held above finely cut, aromatic, fern-like gray-green foliage. It is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established and spreads slowly by rhizomes to form an expanding patch, making it a good choice for a xeric border or meadow-style planting. Deadhead spent flower clusters to prolong bloom, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring or fall.
